headline: The playmakers enter the puzzle arena

image.alt: Nicky Case’s orange cat and Nora Danger’s cream and brown dog mascots experiment with shapes and puzzle grids in a retro-futurist laboratory.
image.caption: Nicky and Nora’s Kaggle mascots take the controls in the Goose’s imagined puzzle laboratory.

sections.heading: Play is the point
sections.text:
Nicky Case and Nora Danger have brought a cat, a dog and a rule-finding machine to ARC. On the ARC-AGI-2 board, the two competed together as kittyhawkarc and irideon. Their Kaggle avatars are an orange cat and a floppy-eared dog; their project, AlexNot, searches for instructions that make puzzle grids behave.

Case calls herself “an educational cat” on Kaggle. She builds things people can play with to understand ideas that are hard to see. Together, Case and Danger have brought that curiosity to the puzzle arena.

The Evolution of Trust is her interactive guide to the game theory of cooperation. It puts the controls in the reader’s hands. Case’s Adventures with Anxiety puts the player in the role of anxiety itself. Her tools make learning something you do, not just something you read.

sections.heading: Triangles, squares and the shape of a society
sections.text:
In Parable of the Polygons, made with Vi Hart, Case lets readers move unhappy triangles and squares around a neighbourhood. Each shape follows a small preference about its neighbours. As the pieces move, the whole community can split apart. The point lands because the reader has just watched the rules at work.

That gift for turning an abstract system into a playground runs through her catalogue: news cycles in We Become What We Behold, game theory in The Evolution of Trust, and a tool called NUTSHELL for making explanations expand on demand. Case makes her projects available for others to reuse and remix.

sections.heading: The CPU rule finder joins the team
sections.text:
Case and Danger’s AlexNot is a symbolic rule finder. It searches for short programs that explain the example grids and runs on CPUs; the authors report about half a minute of CPU time per task on their test machine. On the ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation set, the authors report that AlexNot alone scored 13.33%. Tufa Labs put large models to work. Domdolus Tolus ran its model across four Kaggle L4 GPUs.

Their competition notebook hands the job to an orchestrator called the_boss.py. It runs AlexNot over the puzzles first, then sends the puzzles through their adapted version of the 2025 NVARC system by Ivan Sorokin and Jean-François Puget, running on four L4 GPUs. When AlexNot finds a program that gets every demonstration right, its answer takes the first attempt and NVARC’s top answer takes the second; otherwise NVARC supplies both. Case and Danger also give readers the code and an illustrated paper explaining their experiment.

Case has spent years handing curious readers the controls. What will the educational cat make playable next?
